newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: MEDIATION TO END TSUMEB STRIKE BEGINS.
newsitem.headline: MEDIATION TO END TSUMEB STRIKE BEGINS.

text.p: Mediation talks began on Friday in the hope of settling a bitter six-week old strike at Tsumeb Corp Ltd (TCL) in Namibia, a management source said.
He told Reuters by telephone from Namibia that a group of security guards, trapped for three days without food, had been freed and colleagues had taken over their duties.
"They have managed to do a shift change," the source said.
The approximately 30 guards had been trapped since Monday, blockaded by armed strikers from the Mineworkers' Union of Namibia (MUN).
Management had been unwilling to withdraw them, and their dogs, as that would surrender the site totally into the hands of the strikers.
Mine manager Tony de Beer and his family had also been trapped in their own home since Tuesday morning and had only been freed on Thursday.
The strike over wage increases exploded into crisis this week after MUN members took control of the group's three mines -- Otjihase, Kombat and Tsumeb.
But TCL put forward a new proposal on Thursday afternoon and seven hours of talks followed, mediated by the Namibian government.
The negotiations began again on Friday and were set to go on into the night. "We are hoping some sort of resolution might be reached by some time this evening," the source said.
He declined to give any details of the new proposal.
Efforts by Namibian government ministers earlier this week failed to persuade the strikers to put down their weapons, which included shot-guns and pangas (large knives).
The strikers remain armed and in control of all three mines, but the knife-edge atmosphere is starting to show the first tentative signs of abating, the source said.
"Things have cooled down a bit now," he said.
But he added that there were no plans to try and take back the mines except through discussion. "We don't want to inflame anything," the source said.

Tsumeb mines and smelters, owned by Goldfields of Namibia, have been shut down since August 23. The strike is costing TCL some 80 tonnes a day in lost copper production and a similar amount in lost lead.
